History interventions on training prefixes—deleting, shuffling, truncating, or replacing interactions—can establish that a fitted model’s scores depend on those inputs. If the prefix–target examples already contributed to fitting, improved ranking with intact histories cannot distinguish memorization from generalization. This is a methodological inference: perturbation sensitivity measures model behavior, not independent predictive validity or causal effects on users. Counterfactual explanation research likewise studies recommendation changes under modified histories; such changes alone do not establish usefulness on unseen targets ([CETD](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/20/11176)). BERT4Rec requires masked-target training and an appended mask for next-item inference; bidirectional shifted-target inputs can expose the answer ([BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690)).

Stronger evidence is paired evaluation on untouched validation next-item targets: compare intact histories against shuffled order, recent-item removal, truncation, and matched replacement histories, holding targets, candidates, filtering, and ranking procedures fixed. Report per-category and macro HR@10 differences, with paired uncertainty estimates. Intact-history gains support useful history dependence on held-out examples; gains over shuffling specifically support useful order information. Perturbations may create unrealistic histories, so interpret these as predictive ablations rather than causal user counterfactuals. Repeated validation-guided selection also limits independence; reserve final claims for the host’s untouched held-out evaluation. Preserve the mandated benchmark splits throughout this search, while acknowledging that temporal leakage can affect the broader interpretation of sequential-recommendation results ([Le et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3759329)).
